comments.author: @roy-i3h8d
comments.text:
I genuinely don't understand the hype about Uruguay. The country suffers from outdated infrastructure, and its transportation system feels 50 years behind what many modern cities offer today. Compare that with Panama, which has a modern and expanding metro system connecting the airport, as well as ambitious monorail and rail projects.

Uruguay is also remarkably expensive due to excessive bureaucracy, limited competition, a small population, high taxes on consumer goods, and a lack of economies of scale. Add concerns about organized crime, inefficient local administrations, dirty streets, and graffiti-covered public spaces, and it's hard to see what justifies the praise.

Where is the hype? From my perspective, Uruguay appears to be stuck in the past.

comments.author: @BeyondTheMapTV1
comments.text: Uruguay is interesting because its identity seems built around things that rarely look dramatic on camera: mate, long conversations, quiet neighborhoods, cattle country and a slower daily rhythm. 🇺🇾🧉 Yet behind that calm image is a country with some unusually early social reforms and a very distinctive political and cultural history. Sometimes the places that appear least extreme reveal the most interesting differences in how people choose to live.

replies.author: @PrimeTravel2
replies.text: Beautifully said! That’s exactly what makes Uruguay so special: the calm on the surface and the fascinating history behind it. Thanks for this great comment! 🇺🇾
